cf.title: Add tests for concurrent DML retry paths in logical replication apply

input.subject: Add tests for concurrent DML retry paths in logical replication apply

verdict_reasoning: No objection to the tests survived: the coverage report shows the retry paths are untested, and injection points cost production builds nothing. The two surviving objections, maintenance-fit-1 and maintenance-fit-2, concern only the bundled slot cleanup in execReplication.c. It has no measured gain, and its safety argument in message #5 rests on heap buffer pins and is unconfirmed by any reviewer. Both are fixable, most directly by the split the author already offers.

brief.title: Add tests for logical replication apply retry paths on concurrent DML
brief.problem: The retry paths in RelationFindReplTupleByIndex and RelationFindReplTupleSeq have no test coverage, according to the coverage report. These paths run when the apply worker finds that the target tuple is being changed concurrently on the subscriber. The audience is developers of logical replication.
brief.proposed_design: A new TAP test covers both retry paths. It holds an in-progress transaction on the subscriber for the XactLockTableWait path, and it uses an injection point that pauses the worker between finding and locking the tuple for TM_Updated and TM_Deleted. The patch also makes RelationFindReplTupleSeq scan directly into outslot, and both functions now materialize the slot only once, before returning it.
user_visible_surface: New injection point(s) in execReplication.c before table_tuple_lock; the names are not given in the material.
author_claims: The retry paths in both lookup functions had no test coverage.
Earlier materialization is unnecessary because the scan keeps the buffer pinned and both retry paths restart the lookup.
table_tuple_lock needs only the TID, so the slot need not be materialized before the lock.
Dropping the extra slot and ExecCopySlot in RelationFindReplTupleSeq avoids a redundant tuple copy.
The author says these are not major performance issues in practice; there are no numbers.
brief.thread_state: Hayato Kuroda reviewed v1 and v2 and questioned the materialization change; the author answered with v3 on 2026-06-27. Nobody has replied since, and the CommitFest entry still needs review after one move.
unclear: No reviewer has confirmed the author's argument that skipping materialization before the wait and the lock is safe.
The v3 commit message says "an injection point", but message #3 says v2 uses separate injection points for each path.
The material does not say whether the test is stable or how it waits for the paused apply worker.
The author offers to split the tests from the code cleanup; nobody has answered.
The material does not say whether the cleanup changes behaviour for non-heap table access methods.

objections.title: Unmeasured slot cleanup bundled with tests in rarely run apply code
objections.failure_scenario: A committer pushes v3 for its tests. The removed materialization later turns out to matter in some case, and an apply worker on a subscriber writes a row built from stale or wrong values. Users see this as silent divergence between publisher and subscriber, long after the commit.
objections.argument: The tests add coverage at no runtime cost, but the execReplication.c cleanup changes behaviour in the conflict path that the tests are meant to protect. Message #1 says the gain is not a "major performance issue in practice", and there are no numbers. In message #4 the only reviewer questioned the materialization change, and nobody has confirmed the reply in message #5. The author offers to split the patch in message #5, and nobody has answered.
objections.author_must_show: Can the tests be committed first, with the cleanup as a separate patch backed by numbers or a concrete reason beyond consistency?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 states the gain is small, no numbers exist, and no reviewer confirmed the safety argument in message #5. The author's offer to split the patch supports the request and remains unanswered.

objections.title: Safety argument for dropping materialization assumes heap buffer slots
objections.failure_scenario: An extension table AM whose slots do not hold a buffer pin is the target of logical replication. After v3, RelationFindReplTupleSeq scans straight into outslot and skips the earlier materialization. The AM author finds wrong or invalid tuple data only when replicated updates misbehave in the field.
objections.argument: Message #5 justifies the change by the pin that TTSOpsBufferHeapTuple keeps and by clock-sweep behaviour, which are heap and buffer-manager facts. execReplication.c works through the table AM API, so the invariant has to hold for any AM slot type, and also when the caller's outslot type differs from the scan slot type. Before v3, ExecCopySlot hid that difference. The proposal does not say why the change is safe outside heap.
objections.author_must_show: Why does skipping materialization and scanning directly into outslot stay correct for any table AM slot type, including when outslot differs from the AM's own slot type?

critic.reasoning: Message #5 argues only from heap buffer pins, so the request for an argument that holds for any table AM stands. The slot-type part is weak, because RelationFindReplTupleByIndex already scans directly into outslot, and should not be used as support.

refuted.title: Slot cleanup in execReplication.c has no shown benefit
refuted.failure_scenario: A committer pushes v3 for the tests, and the materialization change ships with it. If the pinned-buffer argument fails for some table AM or slot type, every subscriber can be affected. Users would find out from a wrong or failed apply in the field, in return for no measured gain.
refuted.argument: Message #1 says the cleanup does not fix a major performance issue in practice, and no numbers are given. Message #4 notes that no errors were reported against the current code. Message #4 also questioned the change, and message #5 is the author's answer, which no one has confirmed. The tests have value on their own, so the cleanup carries risk to all apply workers for a benefit nobody has asked for.
refuted.author_must_show: Can the tests be committed alone, and what measured cost or reported problem justifies changing slot materialization in the apply path?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1 for the unmeasured cleanup and the split request. Its table AM point is covered by maintenance-fit-2.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: The patch changes slot handling in the apply worker's tuple lookup on the subscriber.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The lookup functions work through the table AM API, and the new materialization timing applies to any table AM's slots.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The patch adds injection points in execReplication.c and a concurrency TAP test that must stay stable on the buildfarm.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: RelationFindReplTupleSeq and RelationFindReplTupleByIndex run for every replicated update and delete; the patch removes a slot copy there.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Can the tests and injection points be posted as a first patch, with the slot cleanup as a separate second patch?
Why is materializing only once before return correct for a table AM whose slots do not hold a buffer pin?
What measured cost or reported problem justifies the materialization change beyond consistency between the two functions?
How many injection points does v3 add, and what are their names, given that the commit message says one and message #3 says several?
How does the TAP test wait for the paused apply worker, and has it run repeatedly without failures on slow machines?

committability.owner_note: A committer who knows the logical replication apply code and tuple table slot lifetimes across table AMs would have to own it; none takes part in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the stability of a concurrency TAP test on the buildfarm and, if the cleanup stays, for the correctness of tuple lookup in every apply worker, for as long as the code exists.
committability.author_follow_up: The author answered each review within days and posted v2 and v3, offered to split the patch, and moved the CommitFest entry forward in October 2026.

priority.reason: The patch is small (about 14 KiB, one backend file and one test) and serves developers of logical replication. The tests can go ahead once split from the cleanup, which needs its own justification.

provisional_note: Without the code, the review could not check that neither retry path reads the slot after the buffer pin could be released, or that the test is stable. Messages #4 and #5 were seen only through the objections.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Lock updated tuples in tuple_update() and tuple_delete()
precedents_retrieved.summary: When tuple_update() or tuple_delete() finds a concurrently updated tuple in read committed mode, the table AM locks the updated version itself instead of returning TM_Updated for a separate tuple_lock() call. Later versions also had update and delete return the old tuple through a slot passed by the executor, which avoids refetching it and helps table AMs with costly TID lookups.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Version 15 was committed in March 2023, then reverted after Andres Freund's post-commit review. He showed that RETURNING could use the wrong tuple, with an isolation test that fails. He also criticised the new API: the ignored wait parameter, tmfd turned into an input, and the LazyTupleTableSlot code. The redesigned old-tuple API came days before the version 16 feature freeze, and he said it was not ready for 16. In March 2024 the author planned to push a revised version, and the visible messages do not show why the entry was finally returned with feedback in October 2024.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I guess this really is part of my issue with this change - it optimizes the rare case, while not addressing the same inefficiency in the common case.

precedents_retrieved.title: POC: Lock updated tuples in tuple_update() and tuple_delete()
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes tuple_update() and tuple_delete() lock a concurrently updated tuple as soon as they detect it, so a separate tuple_lock() call before the read committed recheck is no longer needed. It also simplifies nodeModifyTable.c and removes an extra table_tuple_fetch_row_version() call in ExecUpdate.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last message, from the author on 2022-07-29, said a benchmark showed a small, noisy gain and that he would bring the patch into a more acceptable shape. No later message appears before the entry was returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Parallel tests publication and subscription might fail due to concurrent tuple update
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moves the publication and subscription regression tests out of a shared parallel group so they run one after the other. Both tests run GRANT/REVOKE on the same pg_database row, which can fail with "tuple concurrently updated".
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane found one such failure in a year of buildfarm logs, on v16 and not on master, which is below the project's noise threshold. Running the two tests serially gives up parallelism for that small gain. The serial schedule would likely stay even if someone later fixes the GRANT/REVOKE race. The entry was closed, to be reopened if the failure comes back.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It would be kind of sad to lose all parallelism for these two
tests, and one-failure-per-year is surely below our noise threshold.

precedents_retrieved.title: Logical Replication
precedents_retrieved.summary: Petr Jelinek posted a WIP patch set for built-in logical replication, with publication and subscription catalogs and DDL, a logical replication protocol and output plugin, and apply workers started by a launcher. It also included a proof-of-concept initial data copy, and left out sequences, DDL replication, TRUNCATE, ACLs and full pg_dump support.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The CF manager returned the entry because the newest patch was three weeks old while review was still ongoing. Peter Eisentraut had posted detailed reviews of each patch, Steve Singer had reported bugs such as a crash in the apply worker after column changes on the subscriber, and no updated version followed. Review found no design objection that blocked the work.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The newest patch is 3-week old, so marking this entry as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Persist injection points across server restarts
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a flush function to the injection_points test module that writes the attached injection points to a file, and the module reloads them into shared memory at startup through shared_preload_libraries. TAP tests could then make a process such as the checkpointer wait at an early startup phase, before any SQL connection is possible.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Jeff Davis found the complexity large for one use case, and Andres Freund doubted the direction because tests needing injection points before consistency must be written in C anyway and can attach points in their own shared_preload_libraries entry. The author proposed a postmaster GUC listing points to load instead, then withdrew the patch since one known use case was perhaps not enough.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Tests that require
injection points before consistency also can't wait for injection points using
the SQL interface or such, so most of the stuff has to be written in C
anyway. And if so, you also can attach to injection points in the relevant
shared_preload_libraries entry.

precedents_retrieved.title: Warning for Datatype mismatch between subscriber table and publisher table for logical replication
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes logical replication emit a warning when a subscriber table column has a different data type from the matching publisher column. The goal is to show type mismatches early so users can debug replication problems.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author did not revise the patch after review, and it had not passed CI since about mid March, so the CF entry was closed. Ashutosh Bapat had asked for the unrelated file renames to be removed. He also noted that the code maps columns by position, and that it compares type OIDs and names on the subscriber without using the remote type cache.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Since this has not been fixed, and the patch has not passed CI since at least
mid March, I'll close this CF entry.

precedents_retrieved.title: Large files for relations
precedents_retrieved.summary: The first plan stored each relation fork as one large file instead of 1 GB segments, converted old segmented relations at upgrade and other rewrite points, and later dropped segment support. After feedback the author narrowed it to an initdb --rel-segsize option that sets the segment size per cluster, with the default unchanged.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author dropped the first plan because segmented mode cannot be removed: ext4 limits files to 16TB, and whole-relation files make file-level backups coarser. The --rel-segsize patch then missed v17 over open problems with incremental backup: pg_combinebasebackup and the segment size, and memory use in basebackup_incremental.c that grows with segment size. Peter Eisentraut's May 2024 review found that the patch needed a rebase and that pgbench/001_pgbench_with_server fails with a 64kB segment size. No revised patch appears in the visible messages.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: If I run it with 64kB, the test pgbench/001_pgbench_with_server fails consistently, so it seems there is still a gap somewhere.

precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a "subscriptioncheck" option to vcregress.pl so that MSVC builds can run the subscription TAP tests with one command, like "recoverycheck". Later the thread moved to a documentation patch that describes "vcregress taptest" for Windows.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andrew Dunstan objected to adding more special targets to vcregress.pl, because the generic taptest option already runs any TAP test set with "vcregress taptest src/test/subscription". The author agreed and switched to a documentation patch. Juan José Santamaría Flecha reviewed that patch and asked for a typo fix and new wording, and the visible messages show no revised version.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I would actually prefer to reduce the number of special things in
vcregress.pl rather than add more.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. [P1] and [P3] changed the table AM tuple_update and tuple_delete API so it locks updated tuples, and their recorded reasons (wrong RETURNING tuple, API shape) do not apply to apply-worker tests plus slot cleanup in execReplication.c. The thread does not point to an earlier discussion of this idea.

The proposal adds no SQL syntax, GUC, catalog object, psql feature or dump output. It changes no user-visible behaviour: it adds a TAP test, developer-only injection points, and an internal cleanup in execReplication.c. The safety of skipping materialization before the wait and the lock, including for non-heap table access methods, belongs to the design angle.

The proposal adds a TAP test, injection points and a slot-handling cleanup inside the apply worker's tuple lookup; it changes no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, protocol message or extension-facing signature. The rows the subscriber applies stay the same, so this angle has no persistent or cross-node state to object to; the safety of skipping materialization is a code-level question for others.

The proposal adds a TAP test, injection points that exist only in builds configured with injection points enabled, and an internal cleanup of slot handling in the apply worker. It adds no SQL surface, privilege, setting or monitoring output, and gives unprivileged users no new action or view. Whether skipping materialization is safe is a data-safety question for the design angle, not a privilege one.
The test part alone raises no maintenance objection from this angle. Injection points compile out of production builds, and the patch adds no hot-path cost for non-users.

No existing feature, test or extension covers these retry paths; the coverage report cited in message #1 shows them untested. The patch uses injection points and TAP tests, the project's existing tools for this, and adds no second mechanism. [P1] and [P3] concern a table AM API change and do not apply.
The tests have clear developer value: the coverage report shows the retry paths are not exercised, and a test-only injection point costs users little. The objection covers only the bundled cleanup.
